output.brief: The evidence points to the revised merit scholarship schedule, not the Admissions Office, as the main reason for the drop. Applications and admits rose, and student quality held steady, so the pool is not the problem. Yield fell sharply only in the tiers whose awards were cut (Dean's $14,000 to $9,000, Merit $9,000 to $5,000). It was flat for Presidential awards (unchanged) and for students with no merit award. Early-action yield fell by about the same amount as regular-decision yield (about 7.5 points each), even though early-action decisions were on time and used the old system. So the portal delay cannot be the main cause, though it was real and probably cost some students. Whether missing-document problems occurred remains unverified. I'm fairly confident, but this is based on patterns in the data, not on direct reports from students. Next steps: don't replace the director on this basis. Take the scholarship schedule back to the finance committee, with the revenue trade-off modelled, before award letters go out. Set a regular-decision turnaround target. Hold off on the vendor rebuild until the transcript problem is checked. Ideally, also check the survey of students who declined.
